# Introduction

Bray-Curtis and its relatives compare metaproteomes by accession: two
different proteins count as unrelated even when they share fold and function.
`repdist` compares them in the representation space of a protein language
model, by default TM-Vec, where the cosine similarity of two proteins is their
predicted TM-score. It does three things:

- **Compare samples.** `sample_mmd()` gives a sample-by-sample distance, the
    maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), for PERMANOVA and ordination.
- **Group proteins.** `protein_similarity()` and `bin_proteins()` cluster
    structurally similar proteins into bins by Markov clustering (MCL).
- **Find what changed.** `bin_glom()` sums counts within bins, for
    differential abundance with any count-based method.

You need protein sequences (a FASTA file, named by protein ID), a count table
with samples in rows and proteins in columns, and sample metadata. This
vignette runs the workflow on simulated data with a known answer. The
[simulation page](https://yixuan39.github.io/repdist/simulation.html)
benchmarks it over many such contrasts, and the
[case study](https://yixuan39.github.io/repdist/case_study.html) applies it to
a real metaproteome.

# Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
# dependencies = TRUE also installs vegan, ggplot2, Rtsne and DESeq2, used below
BiocManager::install("repdist", dependencies = TRUE)
```

```{r libs}
library(repdist)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Data

`simulate_ec` holds 1,160 bacterial and archaeal Swiss-Prot enzymes with
experimentally supported EC numbers: every enzyme of two classes, EC 2.7.7
(nucleotidyltransferases) and EC 2.3.2 (aminoacyltransferases), and 1,000
other enzymes as background. Every enzyme has a positive expected abundance
in each of 20 samples. In each sample of group A, 5% of the abundance goes to
two extra EC 2.7.7 enzymes; in group B, to two EC 2.3.2 enzymes. No two
enriched enzymes share a 50%-identity sequence cluster, so no two samples of
a group share an enriched protein or sequence family: the groups differ in
function, not in any shared protein. The
[simulated data page](https://yixuan39.github.io/repdist/simulation_data.html)
shows how the dataset was built.

```{r data}
data(simulate_ec, package = "repdist")
proteins <- simulate_ec$proteins # sequences, embeddings in mcols()$embedding
counts <- simulate_ec$counts # samples x proteins
samples <- simulate_ec$samples
annotation <- simulate_ec$annotation # EC labels and the truth
dim(counts)
table(samples$group, samples$enriched_ec3)
```

# Embeddings

On your own data, `embed_proteins()` embeds the sequences. Python, conda and
git do not need to be installed: the first call sets up a private, pinned
Python environment (up to a few GB, once). Embeddings made with the `tmvec`
command-line tool are read with `read_embeddings()` instead. `simulate_ec`
ships with its embeddings.

```{r embed, eval = FALSE}
proteins <- embed_proteins("proteins.fasta")
proteins <- read_embeddings("proteins.npz", "proteins.fasta")
```

# Beta diversity

`sample_mmd()` compares the samples' abundance-weighted distributions over
the embeddings. Bray-Curtis compares shared proteins, or shared sequence
families when the counts are first summed within MMseqs2 clusters at 30%
identity (`annotation$mmseqs30`). PERMANOVA (`adonis2()`) tests whether the
groups differ.

```{r beta}
relative <- counts / rowSums(counts)
# summed within 30%-identity MMseqs2 clusters
mmseqs30 <- t(rowsum(t(relative), annotation[colnames(relative), "mmseqs30"]))
D <- list(
    MMD = sample_mmd(relative, proteins),
    `Bray-Curtis, MMseqs2 30%` = vegdist(mmseqs30, "bray"),
    `Bray-Curtis, protein` = vegdist(relative, "bray")
)
perm <- t(vapply(D, function(Dk) {
    set.seed(1)
    a <- adonis2(Dk ~ group, data = samples, permutations = 999)
    c(R2 = a$R2[1], p = a$`Pr(>F)`[1])
}, numeric(2)))
round(perm, 3)
```

```{r pcoa}
#| fig.width: 9
#| fig.height: 3.8
#| fig.alt: "PCoA of MMD and two Bray-Curtis distances, 95% group ellipses"
pcoa <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(D), function(k) {
    pc <- cmdscale(D[[k]], k = 2, eig = TRUE)
    pct <- round(100 * pc$eig[1:2] / sum(pc$eig[pc$eig > 0]))
    data.frame(samples, PCo1 = pc$points[, 1], PCo2 = pc$points[, 2],
        distance = sprintf("%s\nPCo1 %d%%, PCo2 %d%%", k, pct[1], pct[2]))
}))
pcoa$distance <- factor(pcoa$distance, unique(pcoa$distance))
ggplot(pcoa, aes(PCo1, PCo2, colour = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    stat_ellipse(level = 0.95) + # 95% data ellipse per group
    facet_wrap(~distance, scales = "free") +
    theme_bw()
```

MMD separates the groups and Bray-Curtis does not, on proteins or on sequence
clusters: no enriched protein is shared, and the 40 enriched enzymes fall in 37
different 30% clusters, so to Bray-Curtis every enrichment looks like noise.
MMD credits enzymes of one class for being close in the embedding space.

# Protein clusters

`protein_similarity()` joins two proteins when their predicted TM-score is at
least 0.7 and their alignment covers at least half of both, and
`bin_proteins()` splits that graph by MCL.

```{r bins}
S <- protein_similarity(proteins) # gated predicted TM-scores
bins <- bin_proteins(S) # Markov clustering
sizes <- lengths(bins$clusters)
table(cut(sizes, c(0, 1, 2, 5, 10, Inf), c("1", "2", "3-5", "6-10", ">10")))
```

`plot_tsne()` draws the embeddings in two dimensions, here coloured by the 12
largest bins. Each bin is a tight group of points; t-SNE keeps neighbourhoods,
not the distances between them.

```{r tsne}
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.alt: "t-SNE of the protein embeddings, the 12 largest bins coloured"
set.seed(1)
plot_tsne(proteins, color = bins$membership)
```

The EC labels were not used to build the bins, so they can check them: the
share of multi-member bins whose enzymes all share one EC3 class.

```{r purity}
ec3 <- setNames(annotation$ec3, annotation$protein)
multi <- bins$clusters[sizes > 1]
mean(vapply(multi, function(m) length(unique(ec3[m])) == 1, logical(1)))
```

The [simulation page](https://yixuan39.github.io/repdist/simulation.html)
scores the bins in full: purity, pairwise precision, recall, specificity, F1
and coverage, against MMseqs2 sequence clusters.

# Differential abundance

`bin_glom()` sums the counts within each bin, and the bin table goes to any
count-based method; here DESeq2.

```{r deseq}
library(DESeq2)
bin_counts <- bin_glom(counts, bins) # samples x bins
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(t(bin_counts), samples, ~group)
dds <- DESeq(dds, quiet = TRUE)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("group", "B", "A"))
res <- res[order(res$padj), ]
head(as.data.frame(res)[, c("baseMean", "log2FoldChange", "padj")], 3)
```

One bin is significant. Its members, with the truth:

```{r top-bin}
top <- bins$clusters[[rownames(res)[1]]]
annotation[top, c("name", "ec4", "enriched_in")]
enriched <- annotation$protein[!is.na(annotation$enriched_in)]
length(unique(bins$membership[enriched])) # bins holding the 40 enriched
```

All four are EC 2.3.2 enzymes enriched in group B, each in a different
sample. The other enriched enzymes are spread over many bins, so a bin-level
test finds only the part of the signal that MCL gathers into one bin; MMD
above tests the whole of it.

# Notes

`protein_similarity()` and `sample_mmd()` hold protein-by-protein matrices,
so on real data use the proteins identified in your samples, never a whole
search database: 20,000 proteins take about 3 GB each. Structural similarity
does not guarantee shared function: proteins of unrelated folds can catalyse
the same reaction, and `repdist` measures structure.
